lessons.title: Read your first table
lessons.summary: Choose individual columns with SELECT, or use * to inspect every column.
lessons.explanation: Choose individual columns with SELECT, or use * to inspect every column. FROM identifies the table.

lessons.title: Filter with purpose
lessons.summary: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition.
lessons.explanation: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition. Combine conditions with AND or OR; wrap text values in single quotes.

lessons.title: Sort and limit results
lessons.summary: ORDER BY sorts ascending by default.
lessons.explanation: ORDER BY sorts ascending by default. DESC reverses the order. LIMIT restricts how many rows are returned.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;

lessons.title: Find unique values
lessons.summary: DISTINCT removes duplicate combinations of the selected columns.
lessons.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate combinations of the selected columns. Select only cohort to see the unique cohorts.

lessons.title: Summarize your data
lessons.summary: GROUP BY creates one result per group.
lessons.explanation: GROUP BY creates one result per group. COUNT counts rows and AVG calculates the mean of non-null values.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT cohort, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort;

lessons.title: Filter grouped results
lessons.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate values have been calculated.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT cohort, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort HAVING AVG(score) >= 85;

lessons.title: Connect related tables
lessons.summary: INNER JOIN returns matches from both tables.
lessons.explanation: INNER JOIN returns matches from both tables. Match students.id to enrollments.studentId to connect a student with their courses.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT s.name, e.course FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.studentId;

lessons.title: Keep unmatched records
lessons.summary: LEFT JOIN preserves all left-side records.
lessons.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves all left-side records. Count a right-side column rather than COUNT(*) to count zero for unmatched rows.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.studentId) AS enrollment_count FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.title = e.course GROUP BY c.title;

lessons.title: Compare against a subquery
lessons.summary: A scalar subquery returns one value.
lessons.explanation: A scalar subquery returns one value. Use an aggregate in a subquery to compare each student against the overall average.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM students);

lessons.title: Organize a multi-step query
lessons.summary: WITH names a temporary result for the duration of one query.
lessons.explanation: WITH names a temporary result for the duration of one query. Use descriptive names to make multi-step analysis easier to read.
lessons.exampleSql: WITH high_scores AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE score >= 85) SELECT * FROM high_scores;

lessons.title: Express business rules
lessons.summary: CASE WHEN evaluates conditions in order.
lessons.explanation: CASE WHEN evaluates conditions in order. ELSE provides a default. END closes the expression, and AS gives the result a clear name.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT name, CASE WHEN score >= 85 THEN 'high' ELSE 'standard' END AS band FROM students;

lessons.title: Build a cohort report
lessons.summary: Combine grouping, aggregate filters, and sorting in one report.
lessons.explanation: Combine grouping, aggregate filters, and sorting in one report. SQL evaluates row filters, groups, group filters, then the final ordering.
lessons.exampleSql: SELECT cohort, COUNT(*) AS student_count, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY average_score DESC;

exercises.question: Return every student.
hints: Choose individual columns with SELECT, or use * to inspect every column. FROM identifies the table.

exercises.question: Return students with a score of at least 85.
hints: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition. Combine conditions with AND or OR; wrap text values in single quotes.

exercises.question: Return the two highest-scoring students, highest score first.
hints: ORDER BY sorts ascending by default. DESC reverses the order. LIMIT restricts how many rows are returned.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2;

exercises.question: Return the distinct student cohorts.
hints: DISTINCT removes duplicate combinations of the selected columns. Select only cohort to see the unique cohorts.

exercises.question: Return cohort and average_score for each cohort.
hints: GROUP BY creates one result per group. COUNT counts rows and AVG calculates the mean of non-null values.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT cohort, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort;

exercises.question: Return cohort and average_score for cohorts averaging at least 85.
hints: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregate values have been calculated.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT cohort, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort HAVING AVG(score) >= 85;

exercises.question: Return each enrolled student’s name and course.
hints: INNER JOIN returns matches from both tables. Match students.id to enrollments.studentId to connect a student with their courses.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT s.name, e.course FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.studentId;

exercises.question: Return each course title and enrollment_count, including courses without enrollments.
hints: LEFT JOIN preserves all left-side records. Count a right-side column rather than COUNT(*) to count zero for unmatched rows.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.studentId) AS enrollment_count FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.title = e.course GROUP BY c.title;

exercises.question: Return students whose score is above the overall average.
hints: A scalar subquery returns one value. Use an aggregate in a subquery to compare each student against the overall average.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT * FROM students WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM students);

exercises.question: Use a CTE named high_scores to return students scoring at least 85.
hints: WITH names a temporary result for the duration of one query. Use descriptive names to make multi-step analysis easier to read.
exercises.solutionSql: WITH high_scores AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE score >= 85) SELECT * FROM high_scores;

exercises.question: Return name and band: high for scores at least 85, otherwise standard.
hints: CASE WHEN evaluates conditions in order. ELSE provides a default. END closes the expression, and AS gives the result a clear name.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT name, CASE WHEN score >= 85 THEN 'high' ELSE 'standard' END AS band FROM students;

exercises.question: Return cohort, student_count, and average_score for cohorts with at least two students, highest average first.
hints: Combine grouping, aggregate filters, and sorting in one report. SQL evaluates row filters, groups, group filters, then the final ordering.
exercises.solutionSql: SELECT cohort, COUNT(*) AS student_count, AVG(score) AS average_score FROM students GROUP BY cohort HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY average_score DESC;
